subject: Chemistry
title: Castle Bravo: The Test That Went Wrong
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Castle Bravo: The Test That Went Wrong.

hook.text: In 1954, the US detonated a hydrogen bomb expected to yield 6 megatons. It exploded with 15 megatons—2.5 times the prediction.

buildup.text: Scientists miscalculated the contribution of lithium-7 in the fuel. They assumed it wouldn't react, but it did—violently.

discovery.text: The fireball was 7 km wide. Radioactive fallout spread over 18,000 square km of the Pacific Ocean.

twist.text: A Japanese fishing boat, the Lucky Dragon 5, was 130 km away. All 23 crew members suffered acute radiation sickness.

climax.text: Public outrage over Castle Bravo helped launch the global movement to ban atmospheric nuclear testing.

punchline.text: One isotope's reaction was overlooked. The blast was 2.5 times too large.

quiz.question: Why was Castle Bravo 2.5 times more powerful than expected?
options: Scientists didn't account for lithium-7 participating in the fusion reaction
The bomb casing focused the blast more than predicted
Wind conditions compressed the explosion into a smaller area

details.summary: The 1954 Castle Bravo hydrogen bomb test at Bikini Atoll yielded 15 megatons, two and a half times the predicted 6 megatons. The unexpectedly large blast vaporized entire islands and spread radioactive fallout over 7,000 square miles.
details.whyItMatters: Castle Bravo demonstrated that nuclear weapons can be far more destructive than predicted and galvanized the global anti-nuclear movement and atmospheric test ban efforts.
takeaways: The blast was 2.5 times larger than scientists predicted
Radioactive fallout spread far beyond the expected danger zone
It motivated international campaigns to ban atmospheric nuclear testing

faq.question: Why was the Castle Bravo yield so much larger than predicted?
faq.answer: Scientists expected that only the lithium-6 isotope in the fuel would contribute to fusion. They did not account for lithium-7 also undergoing fusion reactions when bombarded with high-energy neutrons. This miscalculation more than doubled the expected yield.

faq.question: What happened to the crew of the Lucky Dragon 5?
faq.answer: Twenty-three Japanese fishermen were exposed to radioactive coral dust fallout. They developed acute radiation sickness, and one crew member died seven months later. The incident caused a diplomatic crisis between the US and Japan and intensified global opposition to atmospheric nuclear testing.
